_children.title: ultraDocumentBody
_children.body:
Course Description: 

This course is designed to provide students with the theoretical foundations critical for developing a deep understanding of the state-of-the-art information quality research from the technical, organizational and strategic perspectives. This course will prepare students to work on their thesis, project and conduct research in the field of information quality. More specifically, students will be exposed to concepts, principles, tools and models and techniques that are essential for information quality definitions, measurement, analysis and improvements. Additionally, students will be exposed to most current, cutting-edge research that goes beyond current industry practice in information quality. Three hours lecture. Three credit hours.

Course Objectives: By the end of this course, students will be able to:

  1. Identify, characterize, and state important problems in Information Quality, Technology, and related disciplines.
  2. Formulate and justify research questions based on potential impact, knowledge gaps, theoretical foundation, and prior work.
  3. Identify, synthesize, and critically evaluation literature relevant to an Information related research question.
  4. Describe and select appropriate research design and methods for a research question.
  5. Write a research proposal for a study including appropriate methods to collect, manage, analyze, and report data.
  6. Communicate research plans and results verbally, visually, and in writing.
  7. Formulate dissemination plans for research products.
  8. Engage in critical reflection of one's strengths and professional development needs in relation to design, conduct, and reporting of research.

Text Book Resources:

  • Research Methodology: A Step By Step Guide for Beginners (3rd Edition) by Ranjit Kumar - E-book available in Course Contents.
  • The Incomplete Guide to the Art of Discovery by JE Oliver - E-book available in Course Contents.
  • Answering Questions with Data by Matthew Crump. Available at https://open.umn.edu/opentextbooks/textbooks/737

Computer Resources

Students do need access to the Internet and a device that allows them to keep up with the readings, complete assignments, and to participate in online discussions. Students do not need an expensive laptop for this course. An inexpensive Chromebook is sufficient when combined with the UALR email/google suite is sufficient.

Course Schedule: 

The Full Term Fall 2026 semester runs from August 24, 2026 through December 15, 2026. This class meets Monday evenings 6:00 pm to 8:40 pm via the web (both synchronous and asynchronous (recorded) formats.  We will also schedule in person meetings as needed in EIT 220.

Grading:

  • Class Assignments: Each week we will have weekly assignments to help students reflect and practice the discussion materials presented in class (50 points)
  • Research Proposal: The culminating assignment (50 points) will challenge each student to produce a well written research proposal and 3 minute thesis describing their research idea.

Based on the student's overall score in the course, grading will be on an A: 90 to 100, B: 80 to 89, C: 70 to 79, D: 60 to 69, and F: <60 grading scale. 

Course Format / Instructor Presence

The course will be conducted as a seminar. Both instructors and students should make sure that all assigned preparation and readings are done in advance and that everyone is ready to engage fully in discussing the topics. 

Workload/Attendance Expectations

Attendance is critical in mastering the course material. If you must miss class, please review the recorded lecture as soon as you can to stay current in the course. Students attending the live sections are welcome to make comments, observations, contributions, and ask questions in the classroom. Online students are welcome to email the instructor. After the 10th day of university classes, students who have not attended class or submitted assignments may be subject to being administratively withdrawn by the instructor.

Students should budget about 10 hours per week for this course.

  • 2.5 hours for weekly class attendance and participation
  • 2.5 hours for the weekly reading assignments
  • 2.5 hours for working on the homework assignments
  • 2.5 hours for working on their own research idea and proposal.

Communication Expectations for Regular and Substantive Interactions

In addition to the class sessions, the instructor for this course will have their weekly office hours posted in the Blackboard course shell. Course communications will be done via the Blackboard Announcements and the UALR email system. Students must use their UALR email when contacting their instructors. On weekdays, a student can expect a response to their email or phone message within twenty-four hours, and forty-eight hours on the weekends. Instructors also will initiate contact with the student, so it is essential that that the student monitor their UALR emails daily, review comments and feedback on assignments, and remain actively engaged no less than several times a week in their course(s). The student is responsible for knowing the syllabus, deadlines on assignments, school policies, and all communication from the instructors to him/her individually and to the class as a whole.

Standard Credit Hour Expectations

This course will adhere to the standard credit hour policy. For a 3-credit course, students can expect 2.5 hours per week of direct faculty instruction including in-class assessment and exams (midterms and final) and 6 to 10 hours per week of out-of-class time (e.g., studying, reading, completing assignments, working on projects, etc.).

Instructor’s Late Work/Exam Make-Up Policy

Unless otherwise specified in class, work will be due on the date given on the class web-page or on the assignment itself. Exercises that are more than 2 weeks late may not be accepted Major Assignments (Research Proposal) are subject to late penalties if submitted more than 1 week after the due date. Students encountering medical or other issues may request an extension at the discretion of the instructor.

UA Little Rock Plagiarism/Academic Policies

Plagiarism on any assignment (including take home exams) will at a minimum result in 0 points for the assignment. We reserve the right to pursue further disciplinary action if appropriate (e.g. student may be referred to the Dean of Students for further remediation). Plagiarism includes copying someone else’s work and claiming it as your own, or collaborating excessively with another person or persons and claiming the work as solely your own. It is strongly recommended that students maintain a record of the preparation of their major assignments. For more information on academic offenses, please refer to the following websites:

  • Academic Integrity and Grievance Policy - https://ualr.edu/deanofstudents/section-vii-administration/academic-integrity-grievance-policy/
  • Academic Offenses: https://ualr.edu/deanofstudents/section-vii-administration/academic-offenses/

Grievances:

If you are experiencing other grievances with the class, be sure to raise these issues first with your instructors and if unresolved, with the Chair of the Department, followed by the College Dean. If the issue is still unresolved, you can file a student complaint at https://ualr.edu/deanofstudents/student-complaints/ 

Inclement Weather Policy

During inclement weather, UA Little Rock will make a decision whether or not to close based on all available information. The chancellor will decide whether or not conditions warrant canceling classes and activities and closing the campus or whether classes and activities will be canceled but with specified campus offices open. Online or web-enhanced classes will continue as scheduled at the discretion of the faculty member. The UA Little Rock website, UA Little Rock email, the university’s main telephone number (501.569.3000), and the Rave campus alert notification system are the official means of communicating information concerning weather-related closings. When necessary, the university will announce a separate decision about canceling night classes (those classes starting at 4:20 p.m. or later) by 2 p.m., if possible. For further information, Please review the Inclement Weather Policy available at https://ualr.edu/policy/home/admin/weather/.

UA Little Rock Disability Policy

If you are a student with a disability, or if you simply want to discuss resources that might help you learn more effectively, you can contact the Disability Resource Center at any time. You are welcome to drop in or call 501-916-3143 to make an appointment. Their staff will work with you to discuss accommodations and identify resources on campus or in the community that might be helpful for you. Accommodations are established through an interactive process. For more information, visit the DRC website or review the steps to request accommodations. We want you to know you are valued, welcome, and wanted at UA Little Rock.

_children.title: Understanding the Research Process Assignment
_children.description: Week 1 Assignment

contentHandler.instructions:
Welcome to INFQ 72203 Information Quality Theory for Fall 2025. For this first assignment, answer these five questions and submit your responses to the assignment folder when done. You are welcome to use Internet resources to help craft your answers.


  1. There are many definitions for research. In a sentence or two, how would you explain to someone what is the meaning and purpose of research? Note: If you got your response from the Internet, that is fine. Just include the URL to document your source.
  2. Just like there are many different answers to what is research, there are also many ways to characterize the different steps in the research process. Use the Internet (ex. you can google the phrase "research process steps" and check out the images) to find a research process diagram that you like and that helps you to understand the steps in conducting research. Copy the image and remember to include the URL to document your source.
  3. What is your desired career goal?
  4. How will research help you to achieve that career goal?
  5. What area/topic/issue/problem/challenge(s) are you interested in exploring/investigating this semester? Use the method discussed in "Finding Research Gap" to identify at least two research gaps of the area/topic that you are interested in.

_children.title: Defining a Problem Assignment
_children.description: Week 2 Assignment

contentHandler.instructions:
Students must choose the focus of their research proposal as early as possible.  For this assignment, you need to write up a one-page thought plan that includes the following sections.


  • Introduce your topic.  For example, start with a compelling statistic, a provocative question, or a striking fact related to your topic. Then, provide the broader context of your research field, gradually narrowing the focus to your specific subject.
  • Give as much background and context as you can at this point, such as who could have an interest in the topic (e.g., scientists, policymakers), how much is already known about the topic, what is missing from this current knowledge, what new insights your research will contribute, and why you believe this research is worth doing
  • Outline your problem statement and research questions.  Hint: Check out Writing Strong Research Questions from https://www.scribbr.com/research-process/research-questions/

Submit your write-up to the assignment folder when done.


Need help finding a topic? Remember to review the materials from Week 1 and  Week 2 to help you generate possible ideas.

_children.title: Literature Review Assignment
_children.description: Week 3 Assignment

contentHandler.instructions:
What can you do with a literature review? The web has many articles on the steps involved with conducting a literature review (ex. https://www.scribbr.com/methodology/literature-review/). In addition, analyzing the literature review gives you a wealth of information regarding your research area, including what people are doing, how they are doing it, where they are doing it, when they are doing it, and why they are doing it. For this assignment, you will analyze a 2024 Journal Article that examines the Literature on "How Educators are Teaching AI in K-12 Education".


  1. How many articles did the authors review for this paper?
  2. What corpus (collections, sources, conference proceedings of papers) did they examine?
  3. What keywords did they use to find potential articles to include in their literature review?
  4. Describe how the authors organized and presented their findings from their Literature Review.
  5. What do you feel were the major findings and opportunities for further research that the authors discovered from their literature review?

Note: Check out the References. Notice that each reference listed can be matched to its usage in the paper. Also, notice that the author is using a style very similar to IEEE (numbered brackets) with the reference list organized alphabetically (some styles list the references in the order that they are mentioned in the paper).  In this course, you can use any of the major reference styles (APA, MLA, IEEE, etc.) - the important thing is to pick a style and apply it consistently whenever you reference/cite your literature sources.


Submit your answers to the assignment folder when done.

_children.title: Evaluating Metrics (and Hypotheses) Assignment
_children.description: Week 4 Assignment

contentHandler.instructions:
Before you can collect your data and analyze it, you need to figure out what you are going to measure. Check out this article on vaccine acceptance among college students - https://www.medrxiv.org/content/10.1101/2020.12.02.20242982v1.full-text


Read it carefully and pay attention to how the authors document their research study. In order to prove or disprove their hypotheses, the authors needed to define and systematically collect their data. Based on this article, consider the following questions.


  1. What questions did this research seek to answer in this study?
  2. Who were the participants in this study?
  3. What procedures did the researchers use to collect the data for their analysis?
  4. Describe the variables (attributes) that the researchers collected from their survey?.
  5. Describe the different types of analysis that the researchers performed on the data collected from their survey.

Write up your responses and submit them to the assignment folder when done.

_children.title: Study Design Assignment
_children.description: Week 5 Assignment

contentHandler.instructions:
The research (study) design is a strategy for answering your research question. A good research design helps to ensure that your conclusions are valid and align with your research objectives, that your data is high quality and reproducible, and that you are using appropriate analytical tools and techniques for answering your questions. There are many designs out there to support the many different types of research situations. You can see some examples of study designs at https://www.scribbr.com/methodology/research-design/.


For this assignment, you will be answering the following questions about the research area that you plan to use for your research proposal.


  1. Describe the problem (i.e., issue, challenge, opportunity) that you intend to examine for your research proposal.
  2. What are the research objectives/questions/aims you plan to examine to help address the problem you identified?
  3. What types of evidence (data) do you need to collect in order to answer your research objectives/questions/aims?
  4. What methods do you plan to use to collect this data?
  5. What is your tentative analysis plan?

Write up your responses to these questions and submit them to the assignment folder.

contents.title: Week 7 Analyzing and Interpreting Your Results
contents.description: Once you have collected your data (evidence) for your research objectives, you need to correctly analyze and interpret your results.  This week students will review basic analytical techniques and formulate a plan for continuing learning and improvement of their analytical skills.

_children.title: Week 7 Class Materials
_children.description: Here you will find any handouts and presentation materials for this week's unit.

_children.title: What Questions are you seeking to Answer?
_children.description: These are not the only questions you can ask of your data, but this is a good starting point.  Other types of questions may involve determining the optimal solution for a set of conditions (also known as prescriptive analysis).  Note: Use the page down key to progress from slide to slide for this online document.

_children.title: What Types of Data do you need to Answer your Questions?
_children.description: There are other ways of describing your data.  For example, another way to look at your data is whether you are looking for structured data or non-structured (NOSQL) data like text.

_children.title: How to Choose the Right Exploratory Analysis for your Data?
_children.description: This article is a nice start to understanding exploratory data analysis techniques.  You can also check out references like Answering Questions with Data (https://open.umn.edu/opentextbooks/textbooks/737) to further build your data summary skills.

_children.title: How to Choose the Right Machine Learning Technique for your Data?
_children.description: This article provides a nice overview of Predictive/Machine Learning Techniques for consideration.  Remember this article is a start, not a definitive list of all available techniques.

_children.title: How to Test Statistical Assumptions about your Data?
_children.description: Every statistical, data mining, or machine learning techniques has certain assumptions about the data the technique was designed to work on.  Think of it like a car.  Each car has an assumption about the type of fuel it runs best on.  If you have a gas powered vehicle, your fuel needs to be an acceptable type of gas (e.g., not diesel) for your engine to have the desired level of performance.  As you review the different techniques available to you, be sure to read up on that technique to understand its strengths and limitations.

_children.title: Overview of Text Mining
_children.description: For those students working with text in their research.

_children.title: Overview of Image Analysis
_children.description: For those students working with images in their research.

_children.title: Example of Specialty Analytics - Overview of Bioinformatics
_children.description: For those students interested in bioinformatics. Note:  There are many types of specialty areas in analytics, including multimedia analytics, GIS analytics, signal/sound analytics, odor/chemical analytics, and the list goes on and on.   The key lesson from all of this:  Think about what data you can collect and what analytics are available to you  for answering questions about your data.

_children.title: Research Proposal Planning Assignment
_children.description: Week 10 Assignment

contentHandler.instructions:
There is an old saying that goes "If you fail to plan then you need to plan to fail". This is very true for research projects. There is a lot to keep track of during a research project and lots of different milestones that you need to accomplish. This assignment is all about project management for research and you taking the first steps to report your progress to date to Dr. Wu and Dr. Dagtas.


For Tips on Project Management, check out these resources.


  1. Review the information/activities needed to complete the research project proposal. There are a number of resources on the web and you can find a nice overview at https://www.scribbr.com/research-process/research-proposal/.
  2. Review the most commonly used project management tools from https://www.projectmanager.com/blog/project-management-techniques-for-every-pm.
  3. Consider putting together a Work Breakdown Structure (WBS - https://www.projectmanagementdocs.com/template/project-planning/work-breakdown-structure/) to capture the different phases and activities you will need to accomplish to complete your own research proposal by the end of the semester.

Every student will need to prepare a 20 minute progress presentation (7 to 10 slides) to share with the class and submit them to the instructors. Students can voluntarily deliver their presentations in one of the scheduled sessions and receive feedback. If you are unable to attend any of the sessions, please submit your slides.


Presentations will start November 9 and continue November 16 and 23 as needed.  Students will be assigned the date to give their presentations.


Here are the items you will need to cover:

  • Title Slide for the Research Proposal - Include your Name, Title, Date
  • Slide to summarize the problem/challenge that you are going to address.  What are the research questions you plan to focus on.
  • Slide that outlines your research objectives.
  • Literature Review Slide(s) - What is your progress?  What search terms are you using?  What types of information are you looking for? What collections have you been searching?  What are some examples of the best articles you have found so far.  (Google Folder with Articles Collected to Date)
  • Slide Describing Your Research Methods for Collecting and Analyzing Your Data
  • Slide summarizing the contributions (merits) of this research.  Ex. Who would benefit? Who would find this research useful?
  • Slide Summarizing the Remaining Work that Needs to be Done to complete the Research Proposal.

Points will be awarded once you have completed the assignment in class.

_children.title: Final Research Proposal
_children.description: Culminating Assignment for the Semester

contentHandler.instructions:
This is the culminating assignment for INFQ 72203 IQ Theory. Be sure to review how to write a research proposal from https://www.scribbr.com/research-process/research-proposal/. At a minimum, your proposal should include.

  1. Title Page - See https://www.papertrue.com/blog/dissertation-title-page/ for examples
  2. Table of Contents (Optional)
  3. Introduction- See Scribbr (link is located above) for more information
  4. Literature Review (aim for a minimum of 20 articles cited in the body of the paper and the majority of those articles should be peer reviewed).  Remember references reflect the papers that you have read and that you feel have something important to support your research proposal's case (e.g., introduction, how your work compares to others, methods used, novelty of work, contributions, etc.).  Consequently, you need to plan on examining 40 to 60 articles in order to identify the 20 strongest works to include in your literature review.
  5. Explanation of the Data You Plan to Collect, Your Research Design and Tentative Research Schedule.  Be sure to identify any limitations or risks that you anticipate and how you will handle those contingencies.
  6. Closing Remarks.  Be sure to explain the Contributions of Your Research to the Field and how you plan to communicate your research findings to others.
  7. Reference List (Remember to use a reference/citation style like APA, MLA, IEEE, etc. and apply it consistently).  For a reference to count, it must be cited in the text and referenced and contain a link to the article itself to validate the reference.  In addition, make sure you have full copies of all your references in your Google Folder that you have shared with Dr. Pierce and Dr. Wu (see the section below for more details on this).
  8. Acknowledgement of any AI Tools that you used to help brainstorm ideas, generated sources for the literature review, or other content that you used as part of the introduction, research design, contributions. Also, it is fine to acknowledge what AI Tools that you used to format, edit, and improve your writing.

Note: Assuming single space, 10 to 12 point font, your research proposal body should be around 8 to 10 pages.


In addition to your research proposal, you also need to include a link to a google drive folder for both Dr. Wu and Dr. Dagtas so we can verify your literature sources that you cited and referenced in your research proposal.

  • Include a full pdf copy of all articles.
  • Be sure to annotate, highlight, or mark up the sections of the article that you used as the basis of your reference.
  • If referencing a book, you need to provide a link to the full pdf text online (or other proof that you had access to reading the book or relevant chapters).
  • Make sure that each article is cited in your paper.  Consider using APA format (Author Name, Date) to make it easy to align your in-text citations with your article identifiers.
  • Make sure that your reference list has a complete set of information for the article (i.e., correct authors, title, publication source, date, etc.).  Again, use a format like APA to fully document your sources.

Check out https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/academic-program/how-to-write-a-great-research-proposal/ for additional guidance.


Also review the guidelines for appropriate use of AI for this assignment - https://www.aiforeducation.io/ai-resources/student-guide-ai-use
